questions.stem: Explain why management thinking evolved over time.
options: Each idea was an answer to a real workplace problem of its time
Professors developed each idea in university libraries in order to publish textbooks
Governments ordered companies to adopt each new idea as the law changed
Managers wanted more impressive titles
questions.why: Ideas are answers to problems: bigger firms, harder competition, new technology and more educated employees each produced a school of thinking. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the three waves of management thinking in the correct order.
options: Classical → human relations → modern perspectives
Human relations → classical → modern perspectives
Modern perspectives → classical → human relations
Scientific management → systems → human relations
questions.why: ~1900s classical (efficiency), 1930s human relations (people), 1950s onward modern (systems and flexibility). See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the main focus of the classical wave.
options: Efficiency
People's feelings
Flexibility
Sustainability
questions.why: Classical management focused on efficiency: Taylor measured the work, Fayol structured the organisation, Weber made it fair with rules. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Describe Taylor's scientific management.
options: Study each job, find the one best way, train the right worker and link pay to output
Let every worker decide the best way to do the job and share the method with colleagues
Pay all workers the same rate so that nobody competes and the team stays happy
Replace managers with written rules that every worker can read and follow without supervision
questions.why: Taylor's three ideas: better work methods (one best way), specialisation and training, efficiency with incentives. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Identify a disadvantage of scientific management.
options: Boredom and burnout from repetition, and no room for the worker's ideas
Lower quality, because every worker is free to do the job in a different way
Slower training of new workers
More errors in safety-critical work, because the standard steps are never written down
questions.why: Standardisation brings speed and consistency but kills morale and switches off the worker's brain, and breaks when surprises happen. See the table in §2.3.

questions.stem: Identify the thinker who first described the functions of planning, organising, leading and controlling.
options: Henri Fayol
Frederick Taylor
Max Weber
Elton Mayo
questions.why: Fayol (1916) invented P-O-L-C and the administrative principles such as unity of command. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Explain the principle of unity of command.
options: Each person should have one boss
Every manager must command many people
All orders must be written down
The most senior person commands everyone
questions.why: Unity of command — one boss per person — is one of Fayol's principles still used daily. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Describe Weber's idea of bureaucracy.
options: Clear rules applied equally, a defined hierarchy, written records and positions earned by merit
Jobs given to relatives of the owner and decisions made according to the boss's mood that day
No fixed rules at all, so that managers stay flexible and can treat every case differently
Workers choosing their own managers by vote and changing them whenever results are poor
questions.why: Weber's ideal large organisation replaced favouritism with fair rules, hierarchy, procedures and merit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Describe what the Hawthorne studies found.
options: Workers performed better because someone was paying attention to them — not because of the lighting
Brighter lights always raise productivity, so factories should invest in better lighting first
Higher pay was the only thing that raised output; attention and lighting made no difference
Workers performed worse when they were watched, because observation made them nervous and slow
questions.why: Productivity rose when lights went up AND when they went down — it was attention, not lighting. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Identify the three things employees need, according to the human relations movement.
options: To be respected, supported and included
To be timed, trained and paid by output
To follow rules, hierarchy and procedures
To work alone, quietly and quickly
questions.why: Mayo's trio: respected, supported, included — the free management tool is attention. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Differentiate engagement from happiness as the chapter explains it.
options: Engagement is feeling respected, supported and included; happiness is a passing mood
Engagement is a passing mood; happiness is the long-term feeling that keeps people in a job
They mean the same thing, and the chapter uses the two words interchangeably
Happiness comes from the work itself; engagement comes from pay and benefits
questions.why: A pizza party makes people happy for an hour; fair treatment and meaningful work make them engaged for years. See the answer to question 3 in §2.5.

questions.stem: Describe the systems perspective.
options: An organisation is one connected system — if one part fails, the others feel it
Each department should be managed as a separate business with its own goals and results
Each department is a separate business
Computer systems are the most important part of a modern business and deserve the most investment
questions.why: Everything is connected; failures live between the boxes, so trace the chain instead of blaming the nearest person. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Describe the contingency perspective.
options: There is no single best way — the right style depends on the situation, people, environment and organisation
Scientific management is the best way in every workplace once the job has been studied properly
Managers should always use the people-first style, because people are the same everywhere
The best style is the one the manager is most comfortable with, because confidence drives results
questions.why: Contingency thinking: 'it depends' is a serious answer, as long as you can say what it depends on. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Identify today's management challenges listed in the chapter.
options: Globalisation, technology and AI, hybrid work, new expectations
Factories, strikes, lighting and stopwatches
Family businesses, cousins, paperwork and favouritism
Low wages, long hours, no training and no job security
questions.why: Today's challenges are different, not harder: globalisation, AI, hybrid work and employees' new expectations. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Identify the modern example the chapter uses to show scientific management alive today.
options: A fast-food kitchen with the same layout and steps everywhere
A hospital emergency team debriefing after a difficult shift
A start-up design team deciding its own working methods
A family workshop of forty workers who all know each other
questions.why: Every McDonald's has the same layout, steps and target seconds — that worldwide sameness is scientific management. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Select the best-fit approach for a hospital emergency room during the shift.
options: Weber's protocols and Taylor's standard procedures, with Mayo-style support after the shift
Mayo-style flexibility and open debate during emergencies, with written protocols afterwards
No fixed rules, so that doctors can be creative and respond to each patient as they see fit
Taylor's time-and-motion study of each patient, with the fastest doctor setting the standard
questions.why: When seconds kill you want checklists and clear command; debrief and support the humans afterwards. See the table in §2.7.

questions.stem: Select the best-fit approach for a creative technology start-up inventing a new product.
options: Mayo-style flexibility and trust, with light structure only
Strict Taylor standardisation of every task
Weber's full bureaucracy with written procedures for everything
The same rules as a fast-food restaurant
questions.why: You cannot standardise what has never been done; creativity needs freedom, safety to fail and ideas flowing upward. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Select the best-fit mix for a fast-food restaurant with young part-time staff.
options: Taylor's standardisation for the work plus Mayo's warmth for the people
Mayo's flexibility for the work plus Taylor's strict rules for how the people are treated
Weber's hierarchy and written procedures only, since young staff need clear authority
No standardisation at all, so that each part-timer can find their own best way of working
questions.why: The burger process should be identical at every station, but part-timers stay or quit because of how the shift manager treats them. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Classify a delivery app that times its riders and a call centre that gives agents a script.
options: Scientific management — Taylor's stopwatch became an algorithm
Human relations — the app and the script show attention to the workers' needs
Systems perspective — the company is tracing failures across its connected parts
Contingency perspective — the company chose the method that fits the situation
questions.why: Timing work and scripting tasks is Taylor's 'one best way' in modern form. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Classify the problem when a student needs four stamps from four offices over three days to change one section.
options: Bureaucracy where rules have become the goal instead of a tool
Scientific management working well, because every step is standardised and recorded
A human relations failure, because the office staff were not friendly to the student
A contingency approach, because each office treats the case according to its own situation
questions.why: Rules become a problem when nobody remembers why and everyone still enforces them. Smart government keeps Weber's fairness and kills his paperwork. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine the human relations lesson when a shift manager notices a tired employee's effort and the employee's work improves.
options: Attention and respect move performance — the free management tool
Only pay can improve performance in the long run; attention gives a short-lived boost
Watching employees makes them nervous, so the improvement will not last beyond the shift
The lighting and working conditions should be improved before anything else is tried
questions.why: Hawthorne's lesson: employees perform better when respected, supported and included. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse this chain: one missed maintenance inspection → one aircraft grounded → four flights delayed → hundreds miss connections → bookings fall next month. Determine the perspective that explains it.
options: Systems perspective — a technical delay became a marketing problem through connected parts
Scientific management — the inspector worked too slowly and needs a standard time per inspection
Human relations — the crew were unhappy and so the passengers received poor service
Bureaucracy — too many rules delayed the inspection and grounded the aircraft unnecessarily
questions.why: One failure travels across connected parts; nobody 'made a mistake' — the system did. See the airline example in §2.6.

questions.stem: Compare how a weak manager and a systems manager respond to a failure.
options: The weak manager blames the nearest person; the systems manager traces the chain and fixes the cause
Both blame the nearest person, but the systems manager documents the blame in writing
The systems manager blames the customer for the failure; the weak manager blames the supplier
The weak manager fixes the system; the systems manager dismisses the employee responsible
questions.why: Systems managers trace the chain; weak managers blame the nearest person. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says the same style works everywhere. Determine the chapter's answer.
options: No — the strongest answers are mixes chosen by reading the situation
Yes — Taylor's style works everywhere once the tasks have been properly studied and standardised
Yes — Mayo's style works everywhere because people respond to attention in every culture
Yes — as long as the manager is experienced enough to apply the style with confidence
questions.why: The same style everywhere fails. Read the situation, the people, the environment and the organisation, then choose. See the answer to question 4 in §2.7.

questions.stem: Determine the chapter's answer to 'should work always be standardised?'.
options: Standardise the routine and the safety-critical; free the creative and the human
Standardise everything, always, because consistency is what customers and regulators pay for
Never standardise anything at all
Standardise only creative work, because routine work can safely be left to the individual
questions.why: A surgeon follows a checklist and still makes judgement calls. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Determine the better choice for a manager who wants long-term performance from a team: a monthly pizza party or fair treatment with meaningful work.
options: Fair treatment and meaningful work — they build engagement for years
The pizza party — happiness is what matters most and the team will remember it
Neither — only pay affects performance over the long term, and both are distractions
Both are equally effective, so the manager should choose whichever is cheaper this month
questions.why: Happiness is an hour's mood; engagement (respected, supported, included) lasts for years. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Classify a company where jobs go to the owner's cousins and decisions change with the boss's mood.
options: The problem Weber's bureaucracy was designed to fix
A good example of Weber's bureaucracy, with authority flowing from the owner at the top
Scientific management, because the owner has found the one best way to run the firm
The systems perspective, because every decision is connected to the owner's judgement
questions.why: Weber replaced favouritism and mood with fair rules, hierarchy and merit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a factory that grew from 40 known workers to 2,000 strangers in 1910. Identify the problems that produced the classical schools.
options: Communication, coordination, motivation, and productivity and quality
Hybrid work, AI, globalisation and sustainability
Too many managers and too few workers to carry out the actual production
Customers wanting cheaper products and governments demanding higher taxes
questions.why: Instructions reaching 2,000 people, who does what, strangers not motivated, everyone working 'their own way' — each produced a school of thinking. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Select one Taylor idea and one Mayo idea a café manager should keep together.
options: A standard recipe and service steps (Taylor) plus noticing and thanking staff (Mayo)
Timing every customer's visit (Taylor) plus letting staff work with no rules at all (Mayo)
Dismissing the slowest workers each month (Taylor) plus a monthly pizza party (Mayo)
Written forms for every task (Taylor) plus leaving staff alone to get on with it (Mayo)
questions.why: Standardise the routine work; give the people attention and respect. Both are needed in the café. See §2.7 and Exercise 2 task 4.

questions.stem: Analyse the claim that management is harder today than in 1910. Determine the chapter's position.
options: Different, not harder — each era solved its own problem with its own ideas and better tools
Much harder — AI and globalisation make the manager's job almost impossible today
Much easier — computers now do most of the planning and controlling for the manager
Exactly the same in every way, because people and organisations have not changed
questions.why: The 1910 manager fought waste and chaos; today's fights complexity and speed with vastly better tools. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Identify the four problems a factory of 2,000 strangers faced in 1910.
options: Communication, coordination, motivation, and productivity and quality
Taxes, labour laws, customers and suppliers
Hybrid work, AI, globalisation and sustainability
Pay, offices, job titles and holiday entitlements
questions.why: Each of these problems produced a school of management thinking. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Describe the chapter's view of management ideas.
options: Each idea is an answer to a real workplace problem of its time
Ideas are invented by professors mainly so that students can be examined on them
Old ideas are always wrong and should be replaced as soon as a newer idea appears
New ideas always replace old ones completely, so only the latest wave matters today
questions.why: Ideas are answers to problems; that is why they evolved. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Explain why bigger firms needed new management thinking.
options: Instructions, roles and motivation that worked for 40 known workers broke with 2,000 strangers
Bigger firms had more money to spend on consultants, who sold them new ideas
Workers in big firms were less skilled than those in small workshops and needed more rules
Governments forced big firms to change their methods through new factory legislation
questions.why: Growth broke the old informal way of managing. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Identify the main focus of the human relations wave.
options: People and their feelings at work
Efficiency and the one best way of doing each job
Flexibility, systems and reading the situation
Rules and hierarchy
questions.why: The 1930s wave put people first after Hawthorne. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify the approximate decade when each wave began.
options: Classical ~1900s, human relations ~1930s, modern ~1950s onward
Classical ~1950s, human relations ~1900s, modern ~1930s onward
All three waves began together in the 1980s with the rise of management schools
Human relations ~1900s, classical ~1930s, modern ~1950s onward
questions.why: ~1900s efficiency, ~1930s people, ~1950s systems and flexibility. See §2.2.

questions.stem: Identify Taylor's three ideas.
options: One best way, specialisation and training, pay linked to output
Clear rules, a defined hierarchy and written records of every decision
Attention, respect and inclusion for every worker on the floor
Plan the work, organise the people and lead by personal example
questions.why: Scientific management: better methods, trained specialists, incentives. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Identify the thinker who designed the fair, rule-based large organisation.
options: Max Weber
Frederick Taylor
Elton Mayo
Fayol
questions.why: Weber's bureaucracy: clear rules applied equally, hierarchy, merit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Identify the thinker behind the Hawthorne studies.
options: Elton Mayo
Max Weber
Frederick Taylor
Henri Fayol
questions.why: Mayo's Hawthorne studies started the human relations movement. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Explain the phrase 'failures live between the boxes'.
options: Most problems happen in the hand-offs between departments, not inside one department
Failures are caused by the boxes on the organisation chart being drawn in the wrong order
Only the boxes at the top of the chart fail, because that is where the big decisions are made
Problems are always one person's fault, and the manager's job is to find out whose
questions.why: Systems thinking: trace the chain across departments instead of blaming the nearest person. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Describe what a systems manager does when something fails.
options: Traces the chain of connected causes and fixes the root
Blames the person nearest to the failure and makes an example of them
Ignores the failure until a customer complains and then offers a discount
Adds a new rule immediately so that the same failure cannot happen again
questions.why: Systems managers trace the chain. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the chapter's airline example of the systems perspective.
options: One missed inspection grounded a plane, delayed four flights and lowered next month's bookings
A pilot who arrived late once and was dismissed to protect the airline's reputation
An airline that bought new planes and saw its maintenance costs fall the following year
A marketing campaign that failed because the advertising agency misunderstood the brief
questions.why: One technical failure travelled through connected parts into a marketing problem. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Identify the four things the right management style depends on.
options: The situation, the people, the environment and the organisation
The manager's mood, age, title and salary
Taylor's, Fayol's, Weber's and Mayo's ideas
Profit, cost, time and quality
questions.why: Contingency thinking: it depends on these four. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Explain when 'it depends' is a serious answer.
options: When you can say exactly what it depends on
When you do not want to make a decision and need more time to think
Never — managers must always have one clear rule for every situation
Only in creative companies, where there are no routine or safety-critical tasks
questions.why: Contingency: 'it depends' is serious if you name the factors. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Describe the contingency view of Taylor's and Mayo's ideas.
options: Both are tools; the manager picks the mix that fits the situation
Taylor was right and Mayo was wrong, because efficiency is what pays the wages
Mayo was right and Taylor was wrong, because people are more important than methods
Neither is useful today, because both were developed for factories a century ago
questions.why: The strongest answers are mixes chosen by reading the situation. See §2.7.

questions.stem: Describe how the chapter compares the 1910 manager with today's manager.
options: Different problems, not harder: waste and chaos then, complexity and speed now, with better tools
Today's manager has a much easier job, because computers handle the planning and the records
The 1910 manager had better tools, because the work was simpler and the workers obeyed
The problems are exactly the same, because people and organisations have not changed
questions.why: Different, not harder. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Identify what employees expect today that they did not expect in 1910.
options: Meaning, flexibility and to be heard
Only a fair wage paid on time at the end of the week
A lifetime job in one factory with a pension at the end
Strict supervision and clear instructions for every task
questions.why: New expectations are one of today's four challenges. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Explain how AI changes management, according to the chapter.
options: It is a new challenge managers must learn to use, like technology in every earlier era
It makes managers unnecessary, because the software can plan, organise and control
It has no real effect on management, because managing people has not changed
It only affects factories and warehouses, not offices, hospitals or schools
questions.why: AI is one of today's challenges, to be met with today's tools. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a start-up that grew from 5 friends to 120 employees and now has confusion, duplicate work and low motivation. Determine the chapter's explanation.
options: The same growth problems that produced the classical schools in 1910
The employees are lazy
The founders were bad people who did not care about the staff they hired
The product is wrong, so the employees have lost faith in the company's future
questions.why: Communication, coordination and motivation break when a firm grows. See §2.1.

questions.stem: Determine the problem that produced Fayol's and Weber's ideas.
options: Coordination — who does what in a large organisation
Lighting in the early factories
Customers wanting lower prices and better quality at the same time
Workers wanting shorter hours and better pay for the same output
questions.why: Fayol structured the organisation; Weber made it fair. See §2.1 and §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine the problem that produced Mayo's ideas.
options: Motivation — strangers in big firms did not care about the work
Communication by letter to the factory floor
Technology — machines were replacing skilled workers faster than they could be retrained
Taxation — governments were taxing factories more heavily each year
questions.why: Human relations answered the motivation problem. See §2.1 and §2.5.

questions.stem: Select the workplace where Taylor's standardisation fits best.
options: A fast-food kitchen
A design start-up inventing a new product
A university research team
A jazz band
questions.why: Routine, repeatable work is where the one best way wins. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Analyse a factory that standardised every task and now has bored workers and no new ideas. Determine the cause.
options: The known cost of scientific management: repetition kills morale and switches off the brain
The workers are not trained well enough to understand the reason behind each standard
The standards were too loose, so the workers lost confidence in the method
Pay was set too high, so the workers no longer had any incentive to suggest improvements
questions.why: Standardisation trades creativity and morale for speed. See §2.3.

questions.stem: Determine the Fayol principle broken when a nurse receives orders from three different managers.
options: Unity of command
Division of work
Scalar chain
Equity
questions.why: One boss per person. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Analyse a company that promotes the owner's nephew over a better-qualified employee. Determine what Weber would say.
options: Positions must be earned by merit, not family
That is normal in a bureaucracy, where the owner's authority is final
Family loyalty is more important than qualifications in a growing business
It depends on the nephew's age and how long he has worked in the firm
questions.why: Weber's bureaucracy replaced favouritism with merit. See §2.4.

questions.stem: Determine the lesson for a manager whose team improved while she was simply observing them with interest.
options: The Hawthorne effect — attention itself improves performance
Observation always makes people nervous, so the improvement must be a measurement error
The lights or working conditions must have changed at the same time without her noticing
The team was faking the improvement to impress her and will return to normal soon
questions.why: Productivity rose because someone paid attention. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Select the action that makes employees feel respected, supported and included.
options: Asking for their ideas and acting on one of them
A yearly pizza party to thank the whole team for its effort
A bigger bonus for the top seller at the end of each quarter
A stricter attendance rule applied equally to every employee
questions.why: Mayo's trio needs real attention, not treats. See §2.5.

questions.stem: Analyse a hospital where the lab, pharmacy and ward each did their job but the patient waited six hours. Determine the perspective that explains it.
options: Systems — the failure sits in the hand-offs between departments
Scientific management — the staff worked too slowly
Human relations — the staff were unhappy and did not care about the patient
Bureaucracy — too many forms had to be completed at each stage of the visit
questions.why: Everything is connected; failures live between the boxes. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Select the first action of a systems manager after a customer complaint.
options: Trace the chain of events across departments to find the cause
Punish the employee who served the customer so that the team learns the lesson
Offer the customer a discount and move on to the next problem
Write a new rule immediately so that the complaint cannot be repeated
questions.why: Trace the chain instead of blaming the nearest person. See §2.6.

questions.stem: Classify a manager who runs a team split between the office and home.
options: Facing the hybrid-work challenge
Facing a 1910 factory coordination problem
Using scientific management on knowledge workers
Using Weber's bureaucracy to control remote staff
questions.why: Hybrid work is one of today's four challenges. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Analyse a manager who says management today is impossible because of AI. Determine the chapter's response.
options: Every era solved its own problem with its own ideas and better tools — this one is different, not harder
Agree — AI changes so fast that no manager can plan, organise or control effectively any more
AI has nothing to do with management, so the manager should concentrate on people
Managers should ignore AI until the technology settles down and the rules are clear
questions.why: Different, not harder. See §2.8.

questions.stem: Select the modern challenge behind a Dubai firm managing teams in four countries.
options: Globalisation
Lighting in factories
Unity of command
Factory efficiency
questions.why: Globalisation is one of today's challenges. See §2.8.
